title: Over 25% of the Stocks in the S&P 500 Are Down 40% or More. 4 Bargain Tech Stocks to Buy Now
detail:
Over 25% of the Stocks in the S&P 500 Are Down 40% or More. 4 Bargain Tech Stocks to Buy Now
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 2:50 PM CDT 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
NFLX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

With the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) near all-time highs, it may be surprising to learn that more than 25% of the index's stocks are down 40% or more from their highs, as of Oct. 8, 2026. That's a shocking number, but it also gives investors the opportunity to go bargain hunting.

Let's look at four stocks to scoop up today.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Netflix

Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX) shares have tumbled as the streaming giant's growth has slowed. However, there is still a lot to like about the stock.

The company tends to be recession-resistant as a cheap form of entertainment, and it is making a big push with advertising, which should become its biggest growth driver in the coming years. It also has the potential to continue adding subscribers, and it has shown pricing power with its ad-free tier.

Trading at a forward P/E of around 18.5 times 2027 analyst estimates, it's a solid stock to scoop up at current levels.

2. Oracle

Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) has become one of the biggest battlegrounds among artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. The company is seeing major growth in its cloud computing infrastructure business, and it has one of the largest backlogs in the space, at $664 billion as of the end of Q2.

However, this is a company already carrying considerable debt and burning cash. Meanwhile, Oracle has been trying to get creative with its financing, including setting up a separate entity to buy chips and then lease them out. This adds risk, but cloud computing economics are strong and tend to have relatively quick paybacks of two to three years, or even sooner.

Ultimately, Oracle's leverage and beaten-down stock price could give it more upside in the space if the cloud model proves to work, and many great companies are betting it will.

3. ServiceNow

ServiceNow (NYSE: NOW) is a stock that has gotten caught up in the software-as-a-service (SaaS) sell-off in 2026 despite being one of the best-positioned software companies for the age of agentic AI. Its platform is one of the most deeply embedded of any software company, with its solution used to run organizations' entire software stacks and its configuration management database (CMDB) linking the underlying relationships between hardware, software, cloud services, and business processes.

The company has leaned into AI and cybersecurity to drive growth, and it's looking to become an important agentic AI orchestration platform with its AI Control Tower solution. With the proliferation of AI agents from a plethora of vendors, monitoring, managing, and securing them within an organization will become vital, and ServiceNow appears to be the most likely leader in this space. With a forward price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 7.5 times based on 2027 analyst estimates, the stock is attractively valued given its opportunity.

What Did It Take To Hold Cadence Stock?

CDNS

A $10,000 investment in Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) stock grew to about $129,800 over the last ten years, before dividends. That same capital in the S&P 500 reached about $36,500. Looking back, the obvious question is whether investors should have bought the shares. The harder question is whether they could have held them. How many times do you think Cadence stock fell 20% or more along the way?

How Often Did Cadence Stock Fall?

Over the last ten years, Cadence stock fell 20% or more from a closing high seven times. Three of those declines reached 30% or more. The table below compares each drop to the performance of the S&P 500.

The deepest decline is the one shareholders are navigating now. Cadence stock fell 34% from early June to mid-September 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%. The longest recovery period occurred earlier. Following its June 2024 high, the stock spent 13 months trading below that price.

What Was It Like Holding Cadence Through A Fall?

Consider the experience of holding Cadence at its early June 2026 peak. Less than two weeks prior, the stock had finally closed back above its September 2025 high, ending a decline that lasted more than six months. The shares then reversed course, dropping for more than three months until reaching a mid-September low. Cadence stock has not closed above its June high since.

The six previous declines all ended with Cadence returning above its prior highs. Yet investors watching this summer's slide had no way to predict where the price would settle.

Was Something Wrong With Cadence's Business?

No. Cadence's twelve-month revenue rose 5.6% between the June high and the September low, and its operating margin stayed near 31%. During the preceding drop from September 2025 to April 2026, twelve-month revenue increased 7.8% while the margin barely moved.

The bulk of that revenue comes from software used to design chips. Cadence reports this segment as Core Electronic Design Automation, representing 70% of fiscal 2025 revenue. The business continued growing through the latest fall. During its July call, management reported second-quarter revenue up 24% from a year earlier, alongside a record backlog.

The underlying business remained sound during both declines. The stock dropped anyway, an unavoidable reality for long-term shareholders.

title: What Changed For Trade Desk Stock, And What Did Not?
detail:
What Changed For Trade Desk Stock, And What Did Not?
Trefis Team

TTD

GOOG
AMZN
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Trade Desk (TTD) shares fell 76.3% in the year to October 13, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned about 18%. The advertising technology company reported slower revenue growth in each of the past four quarters. In the August 6, 2026 report, growth had fallen short of management's own expectations. How far did Trade Desk's growth fall, and what reasons did management give?

Trade Desk Blamed The Economy And Itself

Revenue at Trade Desk grew 17.7% from a year earlier in the third quarter of 2025. By the second quarter of 2026, that expansion had slowed to just 3.0%. During the August 6 call, management pointed to two factors behind the miss. Executives said economic conditions had made it harder for some of the world's largest brands to grow, and they acknowledged that Trade Desk had not executed as well as it could have.

Part of the decline occurred in August. The Motley Fool linked the stock's 24% loss that month to the second-quarter report missing estimates and the analyst downgrades that followed. Trade Desk's peers didn't share the slump: Alphabet stock, for one, rose about 50% over the same twelve months.

Where Is Trade Desk Losing Growth?

The current slowdown centers on some of Trade Desk's largest advertisers. For the year to date, advertisers outside the top 500 had grown over 50% year over year, according to management. Executives also pointed to cyclical pressure on two specific groups of advertisers: consumer goods makers and carmakers. These two categories generate around 25% of the company's business. Even so, about half of those advertisers were still growing very well with Trade Desk.

In August, management assumed no meaningful improvement in conditions for the third quarter of 2026, with results for that period still to come. The company guided revenue for that quarter to at least $650 million. This compares to $715 million in the second quarter and about $739 million a year earlier. That guidance implies revenue about 12% lower than in the same quarter of 2025, which would be Trade Desk's first year-over-year quarterly decline in at least three years.

What Has And Has Not Changed At Trade Desk?

Bottom-line profit has slipped. Over the past twelve months, Trade Desk's net margin was 13.6%, down from 15.6% a year before. In August, management guided to less profit for the third quarter. Adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure that leaves out several costs, was guided to about $160 million. The company reported $241 million for this metric in the second quarter.

title: Update: US Equity Indexes Fall as Big-Tech Sinks After Hot Inflation Report Lifts Odds of Three Fed-Rate Increases in Six Months
detail:
PREMIUM
Update: US Equity Indexes Fall as Big-Tech Sinks After Hot Inflation Report Lifts Odds of Three Fed-Rate Increases in Six Months
MT Newswires
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 12:49 PM CDT 3 min read
^GSPC
^DJI
^IXIC

(Updates with index/price moves, macroeconomic data, and company/geopolitical news from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes fell after a hotter-than-expected inflation report boosted the odds of three interest-rate increases by Q1 and sent mega-cap technology names sharply lower.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.8% to 26,714.8, the S&P 500 slid 1.2% to 7,712.5, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.4% to 51,472.5 after midday Wednesday.

The consumer price index jumped 0.6% in September, as expected in a Bloomberg-compiled poll, from 0.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core CPI climbed 0.3%, above the 0.2% consensus but in line with August. Overall and core CPI year-over-year accelerated to 3.7% and 2.6%, respectively, from 3.4% and 2.4%, and beat market expectations.

A 9.1% month-over-month surge in gasoline dominated the headline rate, as expected, according to a note from Jefferies. Several upside surprises in core inflation imply that higher energy prices are passing through to non-energy goods.

"Several policymakers have said that they don't necessarily need to rush with a rate hike as soon as October, but this data provides a stronger argument for pushing to higher rates," Thomas Simons, Jefferies chief US economist, said in the note. "Our base case is now, once again, that the Fed will raise rates 25 bps in both October and December, with a bias to keep going in 2027."

The CME FedWatch tool showed that the probability of the Federal Reserve lifting its target rate by 25 basis points in October almost doubled to 44% on Wednesday afternoon. The market now sees a 39% likelihood that the Fed will raise its target rate by another 25 basis points in December, versus 19% a day ago. It assigns a 39% probability of another move of the same magnitude in March to the 4.5% to 4.75% range, up from 30% a day earlier, implying three rate increases by the end of Q1.

Most US Treasury yields jumped, with the two-year rising 3.2 basis points to 4.83%.

All sectors except healthcare, consumer staples and energy retreated after midday. Technology, consumer discretionary and industrials led the decliners. The PHLX Semiconductor (SOX) slumped 3.9% after midday, its sixth consecutive day of declines adding up to more than 10% cumulative.

Among stocks with market capitalization exceeding $200 billion, eight of the bottom 10 were technology names, according to data compiled by Finviz. Dell Technologies (DELL) led decliners, down 11%. Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS), the two banking giants that reported quarterly results Wednesday before the bell, were among the worst performers in this mega-cap category.

Bank of America reported an unexpected year-over-year drop in Q3 earnings as a regulatory settlement charge weighed while revenue missed consensus. Shares slumped 6%. Morgan Stanley's shares slid 3.6% even after the investment bank reported higher Q3 earnings and revenue.

In geopolitical news, the Iran-aligned militant group Houthis vowed to continue attacking Saudi Arabian airports and oil facilities after causing extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.

The front-month US West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract advanced 1.5% to $95.55 per barrel, and global benchmark Brent climbed 0.8% to $106.51 per barrel.

Gold futures sank 1.78% to $4,107.40, and silver futures plunged 6.1% to $55.91.
